summary: For ages 9–11: palaeoart and the evidence/inference boundary. Learners distinguish what fossils reliably tell us (size, the basic posture the bones allow, muscle-attachment scars, and for some species preserved feather impressions, quill knobs or pigment-structure colour clues) from what is informed speculation (skin colour, patterning, most soft tissue, sounds, behaviour) inferred from living relatives such as birds and crocodiles. They calibrate confidence on each claim and see how reconstructions change — e.g. a scaly Velociraptor becoming a feathered, alert, bird-like animal — as evidence improves, understanding this as science updating rather than past 'mistakes'.
misconceptions: 'Dinosaur pictures show exactly what they looked like' — colour, patterning and much soft tissue are informed guesses.
'Old reconstructions were just wrong' — they reflected the evidence then; science updated as more was found.
'We can never know anything for sure, so any guess is as good as another' — inferences are constrained by evidence and living relatives, not free invention.
'Feathers on dinosaurs are artistic fantasy' — many are supported by fossil feather impressions.
'If artists disagree, the science is broken' — legitimate uncertainty allows multiple evidence-consistent depictions.

activities.title: Reconstruction studio: build a dinosaur, rate your confidence
steps: Start from a verified, locked skeleton and note which features the bones directly give or strongly constrain: overall size, basic stance, and muscle-anchoring scars.
Add layers in order — muscle (inferred from attachment scars), then skin and feathers where relevant, then colour and patterning.
For each choice, mark a confidence level: green ('known from bones'), amber ('inferred from living relatives or function'), red ('a guess — nothing like this is preserved').
Write a one-line justification for each amber/red choice, e.g. 'birds and crocodiles have patterned skin, so I inferred patterning' or 'no pigment is preserved here, so the colour is my guess'.
Compare your finished reconstruction with a classmate's and identify where you both had to guess versus where the evidence pinned things down.
activities.insight: Building a reconstruction layer by layer makes the boundary between evidence and inference tangible: the deeper, structural layers are well-constrained by bones, while surface colour and patterning are usually informed guesses.

activities.title: Then vs now: the same bones, a different picture
steps: Examine two reconstructions of the same species made at different times — for example an older scaly Velociraptor and a modern feathered, active, more bird-like one.
Note the broader trend in older dinosaur art toward sluggish, tail-dragging poses and in modern art toward active, tail-elevated animals, without assuming every descriptor fits every species.
List what stayed the same (the underlying skeleton and proportions) and what changed (posture interpretation, feathers, activity level).
Explain what kind of discovery could cause such a change — e.g. finding feathered theropod fossils or feather impressions, or a melanosome colour study.
Argue whether the older picture was 'wrong' or was the best guess given the evidence available then.
activities.insight: Changing palaeoart reflects better evidence, not failure; science revises its best-supported picture as new fossils are found.

activities.title: Interview the palaeoartist
steps: Role-play or discuss with a 'palaeoartist' the questions: 'Which parts of your painting could you defend to a scientist, and which are your best guess?' and 'Why did you add feathers?' and 'How did you decide the colour?'
Capture the artist's answers as a two-column list: defensible-from-evidence versus best-guess.
Identify at least one feature the artist would upgrade from guess to evidence if a particular fossil were found (e.g. a feather impression or preserved pigment structures).
activities.insight: Reasoned speculation is justified by analogy to living relatives and function, and the line between known and guessed can move when rare evidence (preserved feathers, pigment structures) appears.

activities.title: Sort the features: evidence or guess?
steps: Given a list of features of a dinosaur picture — size, posture, colour, patterning, feathers, call/sound — sort each into 'known from fossils' or 'informed guess'.
For the feathers entry, decide using whether direct fossil evidence of feathers (feather impressions or quill knobs on the bones) has been found for that species or group, not personal taste.
Explain in a sentence why colour and sound usually fall under 'guess' while size and basic posture fall under 'known' (because the bones strongly constrain them).
Answer: why is a feathered Velociraptor now favoured over a scaly one?
activities.insight: The same reconstruction mixes well-evidenced features with speculative ones, and feathers can be an evidenced feature (from fossil impressions), not mere decoration.

checkQuestion: A museum shows a brightly coloured, feathered Velociraptor. How much of that picture do scientists actually KNOW from fossils, and how much is informed guessing? Explain which parts are which.
checkAnswer: The skeleton, size, and — now — that it had feathers are known from fossils, because feather traces and skin impressions have been found. But the exact colour and patterning are mostly informed speculation, since colour rarely fossilises. Palaeoart is evidence PLUS reasoned guessing, and it changes as new fossils turn up.
